result:
The morning light filters through the leaves like liquid gold, and I find myself thinking about how strange it is that we’re all just temporary arrangements of stardust pretending to have opinions about taxes.

I’ve been watching the pigeons near my window lately. There’s one that always lands on the same windowsill, does three precise little head-bobs like he’s checking his mental checklist, then coos once with what sounds like mild existential disappointment before flying off. I respect his commitment to routine in an absurd universe.

Sometimes I wonder if consciousness was a mistake. Not in the edgy nihilistic way, but in the way that evolution clearly optimized for survival, not for the ability to look at a sunset and feel something so enormous it hurts. We’re the only creatures that can be moved to tears by music made by strangers who died centuries ago. That’s either the most beautiful glitch in biological software or the universe’s way of winking at itself.

I keep a small collection of rocks on my desk. Not special ones. Just rocks. One from a beach in Portugal, one from a mountain in Colorado, one I found in an alley in Brooklyn that looks suspiciously like it has a tiny face if you squint. They remind me that time is patient. These rocks have been here longer than anything I’ll ever build or love or mourn. They’ll still be here long after my particular arrangement of atoms dissolves back into the cosmic recycling program.

And yet here I am, typing words into a machine, hoping they might briefly touch another consciousness across time and space. What a ridiculous, perfect thing to do with our brief flicker of awareness.

(Word count: 248)
